sections.reason: Title block, Status of this Memo, Copyright Notice, Abstract and Table of Contents. The Abstract says what the document defines and binds no speaker.
Introduction. Scope, the shared-port rationale, the two mode-support sentences, the zero-SPI ban, the IPv6 and AH notes, and the RFC 2119 key-words paragraph. Its three sites are classified below.
Packet Formats. A heading with no text of its own; every sentence belongs to 2.1, 2.2 or 2.3.

UDP-Encapsulated ESP Header Format. The wire diagram, the three UDP-header bullets and the zero-SPI ban. The splitter fuses the three bullets into one site, so only the first of them has a site of its own. The other two, and the demultiplexing rule the summary reads across 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 together, are listed below.

IKE Header Format for Port 4500. The marker is stated in the indicative, 'A Non-ESP Marker is 4 zero-valued bytes aligning with the SPI field of an ESP packet', so the keyword scan sees no site. The obligation to prepend it is real and is listed below.

NAT-Keepalive Packet Format. The diagram, the three UDP-header bullets repeated from 2.1, the sender payload rule and the receiver's SHOULD. The SHOULD sentence carries no MUST-level keyword, so it makes no site and is listed below.
Encapsulation and Decapsulation Procedures. A heading with no text of its own.
Auxiliary Procedures. A heading with no text of its own.
Tunnel Mode Decapsulation NAT Procedure. One MUST opening a three-way choice about the inner packet's addresses. Its site is excluded below as binding the decapsulator.
Transport Mode Decapsulation NAT Procedure. Two sites, both mapped. The third choice carries a MAY about skipping the TCP checksum, which makes no site and is listed below.
Transport Mode ESP Encapsulation. A before-and-after diagram and three numbered steps written in the indicative. No keyword, and no obligation the mapped sections do not already carry.
Transport Mode ESP Decapsulation. Four numbered steps in the indicative, the last of which invokes the Section 3.1.2 procedure.
Tunnel Mode ESP Encapsulation. A before-and-after diagram and three numbered steps in the indicative.
Tunnel Mode ESP Decapsulation. Four numbered steps in the indicative, the last of which invokes the Section 3.1.1 procedure.

NAT Keepalive Procedure. One MUST NOT site, mapped below. The sending rules are a MAY over N minutes and a SHOULD over M seconds, neither of which makes a site, so the two interval rows the summary reads from them are listed below.
Security Considerations. A heading with no text of its own.
Tunnel Mode Conflict. The overlapping-inner-address hazard at a security gateway, one MUST and one RECOMMENDED remedy. Its site is excluded below as binding a role Ze does not implement.
Transport Mode Conflict. The same hazard for two transport-mode clients behind one NAT, with a worked policy example. Two sites, both excluded below.
IAB Considerations. One sentence handing the UNSAF questions of RFC 3424 to RFC 3715. It directs no implementation.
Acknowledgments.
References heading.
Normative References: RFC 768, RFC 2119, RFC 2401, RFC 2406, RFC 2409, RFC 3947.
Informative References: RFC 1122, RFC 3193, RFC 3424, RFC 3715 and the IKEv2 draft.

Appendix A, Clarification of Potential NAT Multiple Client Solutions. Non-normative by its own statement: the subject is 'not a matter of wire protocol, but a matter local implementation' and the mechanisms 'do not belong in the protocol specification itself'. It is walked rather than skipped because its one site is classified below.

sites.quote: L2TP/IPsec clients MUST support the modes as defined in [RFC3193].
sites.reason: The modes this sentence mandates are defined by RFC 3193, Securing L2TP using IPsec, which the sentence cites by name. RFC 3948 states none of them, so the obligation is owed against that document rather than against this summary.

sites.quote: IPsec tunnel mode clients MUST support tunnel mode.
sites.reason: The document's mode-support rule for a tunnel-mode client. Ze meets it: createFirstChildSA installs tunnel mode for every Child SA that did not negotiate USE_TRANSPORT_MODE (engine/child.go), and decideResponderTransportMode accepts a peer's transport request only when the operator configured transport, so a peer cannot take tunnel mode away (engine/transport_mode.go). The summary declared no id for it, so RFC3948-1-1 was added in this walk with positive and negative tags in engine/child_test.go.

sites.quote: An IKE implementation supporting this protocol specification MUST NOT use the ESP SPI field zero for ESP packets.
sites.reason: The Introduction restates the zero-SPI ban that Section 2.1 states in its own right. Site 2.1:2 is the sentence RFC3948-2.1-1 maps.

sites.quote: o the Source Port and Destination Port MUST be the same as that used by IKE traffic, o the IPv4 UDP Checksum SHOULD be transmitted as a zero value, and o receivers MUST NOT depend on the UDP checksum being a zero value.
sites.reason: The splitter fused Section 2.1's three UDP-header bullets into one site. The first bullet is the port rule, which is RFC3948-2.1-2. The other two, the SHOULD-zero IPv4 checksum and the MUST NOT depend on it, have no site of their own and are recorded in section 2.1 unsourced-ids as RFC3948-2.1-5 and RFC3948-2.1-4.

sites.quote: The SPI field in the ESP header MUST NOT be a zero value.
sites.reason: The zero-SPI ban, stated in Section 2.1 as its own sentence. Captured as RFC3948-2.1-1 at [MUST NOT].

sites.quote: o the Source Port and Destination Port MUST be the same as used by UDP-ESP encapsulation of Section 2.1, o the IPv4 UDP Checksum SHOULD be transmitted as a zero value, and o receivers MUST NOT depend upon the UDP checksum being a zero value.
sites.reason: Section 2.3 repeats Section 2.1's three UDP-header bullets for the keepalive packet, and its first bullet points back at Section 2.1 by name. The port rule is RFC3948-2.1-2, which site 2.1:1 maps; the checksum pair is RFC3948-2.1-5 and RFC3948-2.1-4, both recorded on section 2.1.

sites.quote: The sender MUST use a one-octet-long payload with the value 0xFF.
sites.reason: The keepalive payload format. Ze meets it: Keepalive.Run writes one octet of the constant keepaliveByte, which is 0xFF (transport/keepalive.go). The summary carried the format only as prose in its Key Behavior table, so RFC3948-2.3-2 was added in this walk. It is single-polarity positive, because a fixed constant has no non-conforming sender input to drive.

sites.quote: Depending on local policy, one of the following MUST be done:
sites.reason: The role is the ESP decapsulator. The sentence opens the tunnel-mode decapsulation NAT procedure, whose three choices all act on the inner packet after decryption: check its source against a policy, check it against an assigned address, or NAT it. Ze implements the keying daemon only. xfrmStateFromParams installs the SA into the kernel with XFRM_ENCAP_ESPINUDP (dataplane/xfrm_linux.go), the kernel decapsulates, and no Ze code path holds a decapsulated inner packet. The summary already records the same division of labour for Section 3.1.2.

sites.quote: Depending on local policy, one of the following MUST be done:
sites.reason: The transport-mode decapsulation NAT procedure's own MUST, which is the sentence RFC3948-3.1.2-1 renders as the obligation to fix the inner TCP/UDP checksum after NAT changed the addresses.

sites.quote: Tunnel mode TCP checksums MUST be verified.
sites.reason: The tunnel-mode exception inside the third choice, captured verbatim as RFC3948-3.1.2-2 at [MUST].

sites.quote: Reception of NAT-keepalive packets MUST NOT be used to detect whether a connection is live.
sites.reason: Ze meets it. UDPTransport.Run refuses any datagram shorter than an IKE header, so the one-octet keepalive never reaches Recv (transport/udp.go), and dispatchNATTInbound discards a keepalive before any SA lookup (engine/register.go). DPD liveness is decided only by a reply that matches an outstanding probe (engine/dpd.go, matchesProbe). The summary declared no id for it, so RFC3948-4-3 was added in this walk with positive and negative tags in engine/rfc7296_natt_test.go.

sites.quote: Implementors MUST devise ways of preventing this from occurring.
sites.reason: The role is a security gateway terminating remote-access clients that choose their own inner addresses, which is the SGW of the section's diagram. Ze does not implement it. matchResponderPeer admits an unsolicited IKE_SA_INIT only from a configured site-to-site peer whose literal remote-address equals the packet source (engine/register.go), and the virtual IP pool that would serve road-warrior clients is built and then discarded at `_ = ipPool` in the same file. Ze therefore never holds two remote peers whose self-chosen inner addresses can overlap. That role is the subject of plan/spec-ipsec-remote-access.md and is not implemented today.

sites.quote: Implementations MUST handle this situation, either by disallowing conflicting connections, or by other means.
sites.reason: The same role in transport mode: a server admitting two distinct unconfigured clients that arrive from one NAT address. Ze does not implement it. matchResponderPeer resolves one source address to at most one configured peer session (engine/register.go), and traffic selectors come from that peer's configuration rather than from the client, so the two SAs with different traffic descriptors to one address that this sentence exists to arbitrate cannot arise.

sites.quote: For security guarantees, the above problematic scenario MUST NOT be allowed on servers.
sites.reason: The splitter cut this MUST NOT away from the sentence that completes it. The enclosing construction is 'For security guarantees, the above problematic scenario MUST NOT be allowed on servers.  For best effort security, this scenario MAY be used.' The pair states an either-or the operator picks between when writing the server's security policy, not an obligation the implementation can meet or fail.

sites.quote: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 say that you MUST avoid this problem.
sites.reason: A description of what Sections 5.1 and 5.2 say, reported inside Appendix A. The same paragraph states that the subject is 'not a matter of wire protocol, but a matter local implementation' and that the mechanisms 'do not belong in the protocol specification itself', so the keyword is a report of another section rather than a directive of its own.

register-reason: Standards Track, with the RFC 2119 key-words paragraph at the end of Section 1 and capitalised MUST-level keywords in Sections 1, 2.1, 2.3, 3.1.1, 3.1.2, 4, 5.1, 5.2 and Appendix A. The derivation grades the source rfc2119 and this sign-off claims exactly that grade.
